meta.title: Who really said "Art, Like Morality, Consists of Drawing the Line Somewhere"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: G. K. Chesterton wrote it in his Illustrated London News column on 5 May 1928 — confirmed in the scanned issue. Oscar Wilde never said it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Art, Like Morality, Consists of Drawing the Line Somewhere'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Oscar Wilde. G. K. Chesterton, 'Our Note Book,' The Illustrated London News, 5 May 1928 — verified against the scanned original issue.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Chesterton wrote the sentence in “Our Note Book,” his weekly column in The Illustrated London News, published 5 May 1928. The wording that circulates today is his exact printed wording — the sentence appears verbatim in the scanned original issue, under his byline. It is not Oscar Wilde’s.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “it consists in drawing the line somewhere” — same column, 5 June 1920

source.excerpt: Some say that art is unmoral; and some of these arts are very unmoral. I may not have described them here in the correct conventional terms; but then I do not think that art is unmoral. Art, like morality, consists of drawing the line somewhere.
trail: 5 June 1920 — Chesterton first reaches for the idea in the same column, writing that the citizen’s power “is like the power of the artist; it consists in drawing the line somewhere.” The sentence is in the scanned issue ↗, under his byline.
5 May 1928 — eight years later he sharpens it into the line people quote. The scanned issue ↗ carries the sentence in a column headed “By G. K. CHESTERTON.”

Traced — Quote Investigator ↗ assembles the chronology and concludes that Chesterton originated the statement printed in The Illustrated London News in 1928. The Society of Gilbert Keith Chesterton ↗ gives the same citation.
Today — a reworded version travels under Oscar Wilde’s name. The Quotations Page ↗ still credits “Morality, like art, means drawing a line someplace” to Wilde, with no source given.
source.excerptNote: The passage sits in a column mocking the publishing fashion for “Outline of…” books that followed H. G. Wells’s The Outline of History — Chesterton’s joke being that the Outliners are the last people who want an actual outline. The transcription above is Quote Investigator’s; it matches the machine-read text of the scanned issue word for word.

Works first published before 1931 are in the public domain in the United States, so this text may be quoted freely. Note that modern edited collections of Chesterton’s columns carry their own editorial copyright — the 1928 periodical text does not.

author.name: G. K. Chesterton
author.heading: Who was G. K. Chesterton?
author.bio: Gilbert Keith Chesterton was an English journalist, novelist, essayist and poet, born 29 May 1874 and died 14 June 1936. He is best remembered for the Father Brown detective stories and for books like Orthodoxy and The Man Who Was Thursday, but he made his living as a working columnist — a weekly column in The Illustrated London News from 1905 that he kept up for some three decades. That enormous, largely uncollected output is why so many of his best sentences circulate as orphan epigrams, and why they so often end up filed under a wittier-sounding name.

copyAttribution: "Art, like morality, consists of drawing the line somewhere." — G. K. Chesterton, "Our Note Book," The Illustrated London News, 5 May 1928, p. 780. Frequently misattributed to Oscar Wilde.

misattribution.heading: Why people say Oscar Wilde
misattribution.intro: This is a Wilde-magnet sentence: epigrammatic, faintly naughty, built on a pun. So it drifted to Wilde — but in a reworded form, and with no source behind it anywhere.

items.why: Quote Investigator states plainly that there is no substantive evidence Oscar Wilde said or wrote this statement, and that a variant was constructed and incorrectly assigned to him — see the full chronology ↗. Wilde died in 1900; the sentence was printed in 1928.

items.who: “Morality, like art, means drawing a line someplace”
items.why: This Americanised rewrite — clauses swapped, “someplace” for “somewhere” — is the form that circulates under Wilde’s name. The Quotations Page ↗ and Goodreads ↗ both list it as Wilde’s with no work cited.

Plenty of reprints give “consists in drawing the line.” The 1928 column reads “consists of”; “consists in” is the construction Chesterton used in his 1920 column ↗, which may be why the two forms blur together.

misattribution.truthLine: It is Chesterton’s, and the paper trail is short: “Our Note Book,” The Illustrated London News, 5 May 1928 — readable in the scanned original ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line is a pun, and the pun is the whole argument. An artist literally draws lines; a moralist figuratively draws one. Chesterton’s point is that these are the same act — that choosing what to leave out is not a failure of nerve but the thing that makes a work a work at all. Anyone can be limitless. Only a form has edges.

He was writing that week about the publishing craze for “Outline of…” books, set off by H. G. Wells’s The Outline of History. Chesterton found it funny that the word outline had become a favourite of exactly the people least willing to accept a definite limit — and the sentence lands as the sting in that joke, not as a detached aphorism.
detailsBody: Chesterton had circled the idea eight years earlier. In his column of 5 June 1920 he wrote that the citizen’s power “is like the power of the artist; it consists in drawing the line somewhere” — the same analogy, aimed at citizenship rather than morality, and not yet compressed.

He wrote this column weekly for decades. Wikipedia records that a weekly column in The Illustrated London News followed in 1905, “for which he continued to write for the next 30 years.” Most of those pieces were never collected in his lifetime, which is part of why so many Chesterton lines float free of any citation — and why they are so easy to reassign to someone more famous for epigrams.
context.pull: An artist draws a line. So does a conscience. Chesterton thought that was the same sentence.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes G. K. Chesterton originated the statement, printed in The Illustrated London News in 1928 ('Our Note Book', May 5, 1928, page 780), and states there is no substantive evidence Oscar Wilde said or wrote it; QI also documents a June 5, 1920 precursor reading 'it consists in drawing the line somewhere.'

The scanned 5 May 1928 issue of The Illustrated London News (Vol. 172, Iss. 4646) contains 'Art, like morality, consists of drawing the line somewhere' within a column bylined 'By G. K. CHESTERTON', in a passage about H. G. Wells's The Outline of History and the vogue for 'Outline of...' books; the running head reads 'ILLUSTRATED LONDON NEWS ... May 5, 1928'. Verified by downloading and searching the item's OCR text (djvu.txt) and djvu.xml page structure.

The scanned 5 June 1920 issue of The Illustrated London News (Vol. 156, Iss. 4233) contains 'it consists in drawing the line somewhere. The idea of the nation of kings is that every citizen respects every other citizen...' in a column bylined 'By G. K. CHESTERTON.' Verified via the item's OCR text.

The Society of Gilbert Keith Chesterton's Art and Literature quotations page carries 'Art, like morality, consists of drawing the line somewhere.' with the source citation 'Illustrated London News, May 5, 1928.'
The Quotations Page attributes 'Morality, like art, means drawing a line someplace.' to Oscar Wilde (1854-1900) and provides no source citation for it.
Goodreads lists 'Morality, like art, means drawing a line someplace.' as an Oscar Wilde quote with no source work cited.

Wikipedia gives G. K. Chesterton's dates as 29 May 1874 - 14 June 1936, describes him as an English journalist, novelist, essayist and poet, and states a weekly column in The Illustrated London News 'followed in 1905, for which he continued to write for the next 30 years.'
